title: Advanced Search and Dorking: Finding Exposure Before Someone Else Does
intro: Advanced search is the use of operators such as site:, filetype: and intitle: to turn a public search engine into a structured filter over the pages, files and services it has indexed. This lesson teaches you to use those operators, specialized infrastructure engines, archives and code search to find your own organization's accidental exposure and to research known-malicious infrastructure, while staying on the right side of legal and ethical limits.

sections.heading: How Search Engines Index the Web and Why Operators Matter
sections.content:
A search engine does not read the live web when you type a query. Crawlers fetch pages by following links and sitemaps, parse the content, and store a processed copy in an inverted index that maps terms to documents. Your query is answered from that index, never from the target server. Three consequences matter to a defender.

First, anything a crawler can reach without authentication can be indexed, including files nobody linked on purpose: a spreadsheet uploaded to a public folder, a backup left next to a web root, a staging site with no password. Second, the index lags reality. A page removed today may still be returned, snippet included, for days or weeks. Third, indexing is steered by robots.txt, noindex tags and authentication, but the first two are polite requests, not security controls. A Disallow line in robots.txt even advertises a sensitive path to anyone who reads the file, and it does not stop crawlers that ignore it.

Why operators? A plain keyword query is ranked by relevance and popularity, which buries the long tail where accidental exposure lives. Operators expose the fields the engine already stores: host, URL, title, body text and file type. Instead of scrolling through ranked pages, you ask a precise question such as: which PDF files on any subdomain of my company contain the word confidential?

Two defensive uses drive everything in this lesson:

- Attack surface discovery: finding what your own organization has exposed, usually by accident, so you can fix it.
- Threat intelligence: researching known-malicious infrastructure, phishing kits, brand impersonation and mentions of your company on leak or paste sites.

Searching is passive collection. Typing a dork sends nothing to the target, which is why it is the lowest-risk way to start. Opening a result is different: you are now making a request to that server or a third party. For anything suspected to be malicious, use an isolated browser or an archived copy.

Know the limits. Engines cap how many results they return per query, personalize and localize ranking, and change behavior without notice. An absent result is not proof of absence. A present result is a lead, not a finding, until you have verified it.

A useful questioning frame for every result you see:

- Is this asset actually ours?
- Is it still live, or only a stale index entry?
- What exactly does it expose, and to whom?
- How did it become reachable and indexable?
- Who owns the fix?

sections.heading: Core Google Operators with Examples
sections.content:
Operators are written as operator:value with no space after the colon. Most can be combined, and each added operator narrows the result set. The reference below covers the ones you will use daily.

| Operator | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| site: | Restricts results to a domain, subdomain or TLD | site:example-corp.com |
| filetype: (or ext:) | Restricts to a file extension | filetype:xlsx |
| intitle: | Term must appear in the page title | intitle:"index of" |
| inurl: | Term must appear in the URL | inurl:admin |
| intext: | Term must appear in the body | intext:"internal use only" |
| "quotes" | Exact phrase match | "employee onboarding checklist" |
| - (minus) | Excludes a term or operator | -site:www.example-corp.com |
| OR (or pipe) | Either term | filetype:pdf OR filetype:docx |
| * | Wildcard for one or more words inside a phrase | "password for * is" |
| allintitle: | All following terms must be in the title | allintitle: login portal |

A few examples, one per line, each answering a defensive question:

```
site:example-corp.com filetype:pdf "internal use only"
site:example-corp.com -site:www.example-corp.com
site:example-corp.com inurl:login OR inurl:signin OR inurl:admin
site:example-corp.com intitle:"index of" "parent directory"
"example-corp" filetype:xlsx intext:password -site:example-corp.com
```

The second query is a favorite for subdomain discovery. Excluding the main host forces the engine to show everything else under the domain: forgotten dev, test and partner subdomains. The last query changes the scope on purpose. It looks for spreadsheets that mention your company name and the word password but are hosted elsewhere, which is how you find a supplier or contractor who published your data.

Combining rules and pitfalls:

- Operators are case-insensitive but OR must be uppercase.
- Quotes around a phrase beat loose keywords when you need precision, and they also stop the engine from silently rewriting your query with synonyms.
- The cache: operator and the cached-page link were retired by Google in 2024, so do not build a workflow on them. Use web archives instead (section five).
- Old operators such as related: and the plus sign no longer behave as documented. Test an operator on a known page before trusting its absence of results.
- Very long queries are truncated. Split a large keyword list into several smaller queries.

Other engines behave differently. Bing supports site:, filetype:, intitle:, inurl: and adds inbody:, contains: and ip: (pages hosted on an IP address), but its index and ranking differ, so run important queries on both. DuckDuckGo supports a smaller core set (site:, filetype:, intitle:, inurl:, quotes and minus) and draws on other providers, so coverage and freshness differ. Different indexes see different files; a clean result on one engine says little about the others.

sections.heading: Dorking for Attack-Surface Discovery
sections.content:
A dork is simply a stored, reusable operator query aimed at a known risk pattern. Defensive dorking means running those patterns scoped to your own domains and brand to see what an outsider sees before a criminal does. The Google Hacking Database (GHDB), maintained by Exploit-DB, is the best-known public catalog: thousands of dorks grouped by category such as files containing passwords, sensitive directories, vulnerable servers, footholds, error messages and login portals. Treat it as a pattern library, not a script to run blindly. Each entry tells you what class of mistake to look for; you adapt it with site: and your own naming conventions.

Four exposure families deserve a recurring review:

**Exposed documents.** Office files, PDFs and exports that were meant to be internal.

```
site:example-corp.com (filetype:pdf OR filetype:docx OR filetype:xlsx) ("confidential" OR "internal only" OR "not for distribution")
site:example-corp.com filetype:csv ("email" OR "ssn" OR "salary")
```

**Directory listings.** A web server configured to list a folder's contents shows every file in it, including ones never linked anywhere.

```
site:example-corp.com intitle:"index of /"
site:example-corp.com intitle:"index of" (backup OR dump OR .sql OR .zip)
```

**Login and admin portals.** These are not vulnerabilities by themselves, but an inventory of internet-facing portals is the first input to patching and MFA coverage.

```
site:example-corp.com (inurl:admin OR inurl:login OR inurl:vpn OR inurl:owa OR intitle:"sign in")
```

**Misindexed files and configuration.** Environment files, config backups, log files and error pages that leak paths or credentials.

```
site:example-corp.com (ext:env OR ext:log OR ext:bak OR ext:conf OR ext:ini)
site:example-corp.com intext:"stack trace" OR intext:"fatal error"
```

What the result means for the analyst: a hit proves the engine indexed something, not that it is dangerous. Triage each hit on three axes: is the data sensitive, is it reachable by anyone without credentials, and is it still live? A stale index entry for a deleted file is a cleanup task, while a live unauthenticated backup is an incident.

Pitfalls specific to this work:

- False positives are common. Public marketing PDFs legitimately contain the word confidential in a disclaimer footer. Read before you escalate.
- Third-party scope. Dorks that drop site: find other organizations' data. If you stumble onto it, the rule is: stop, record only the minimum needed to identify the owner (URL and timestamp), do not download or share it, and report it through the owner's security contact or your national CERT.
- Automation. Scraping a search engine violates its terms and triggers CAPTCHAs and blocks. Run curated dorks manually or through an official search API, and respect rate limits.
- Authorization. Passive search is generally fine. Logging into a discovered portal with default credentials, even your own company's, without written approval, is not.

sections.heading: Infrastructure Search Engines: Shodan and Censys
sections.content:
Google indexes page text that crawlers can read. Shodan and Censys index something different: the responses that internet-facing services return when the engine connects directly to IP addresses and ports. Think of Google as a library catalog of documents, and these engines as a census of every door on the street, recording what each door looks like and what sign hangs on it. The result is a database of banners, open ports, TLS certificates, software versions and HTTP titles, refreshed on scan cycles.

That makes them ideal for answering questions about your perimeter: which of our IP ranges expose RDP, which hosts present a certificate for our domain, and which devices still run an end-of-life product version.

Shodan filters follow the same colon syntax:

```
org:"Example Corp" port:3389
hostname:example-corp.com http.title:"Dashboard"
net:203.0.113.0/24 product:"Apache httpd"
ssl.cert.subject.cn:example-corp.com -port:443
```

The last query is worth studying. It finds services whose certificate names your domain but that listen on a port other than 443, which often means a forgotten admin interface or an appliance someone published without telling security.

Censys exposes a similar model through a structured query language over host, service and certificate fields. Field names have changed between Censys product generations, so read the current documentation instead of copying old queries. The typical patterns are the same: filter by autonomous system or organization name, by service port, by certificate subject, and by HTTP page title.

```
autonomous_system.name: "EXAMPLE-CORP-AS" and services.port: 3389
services.tls.certificates.leaf_data.subject.common_name: "example-corp.com"
```

Certificate transparency pivots are especially valuable. Every publicly trusted certificate is logged, so searching certificate subject names reveals subdomains that never appeared in any web page.

How to read a result responsibly:

- Check the timestamp. Scan data can be days or weeks old; the service may already be fixed or gone.
- Shared hosting and CDNs mean that an IP in your results may not be yours at all. Confirm ownership through your asset inventory.
- A banner shows what the service claims. Version strings can be spoofed or backported, so a listed version is a lead for your vulnerability team, not a confirmed vulnerability.
- Do not probe other people's devices to verify a hit. Reading the engine's stored data is passive; connecting to a stranger's device is not.

For enrichment of individual indicators (reputation, passive DNS, WHOIS), see the existing enrichment tools lesson. This lesson focuses on discovery by query, while that one covers scoring an indicator you already have.

sections.heading: Historical and Cached Sources: Why Deleted Content Persists
sections.content:
Removing a page from your website does not remove it from the internet. Content lives on in several places that you do not control, and an analyst needs to know them both to investigate adversary infrastructure that has been taken down and to understand the true impact of an exposure.

**Web archives.** The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine stores timestamped snapshots of billions of pages, retrievable by URL. Other archive services take on-demand snapshots that preserve a page exactly as it looked, including a phishing page that the attacker later deleted. Archived copies are the standard way to preserve evidence of a takedown-prone site.

```
https://web.archive.org/web/2024*/example-corp.com/*
https://web.archive.org/web/20240115000000*/example-corp.com/internal/*
```

The wildcard form lists every archived URL under a path. Reading that list is a form of historical directory discovery: you may find an old admin path, a retired API route or a file that was once published and later removed.

**Search engine caches.** Google retired its public cached-page links and the cache: operator in 2024, so you can no longer rely on them. Other engines have kept or changed their own cache features, so treat any cache feature as unreliable and archive what matters yourself, immediately.

**Other copies.** Social shares, forum quotes, link-shortener previews, scrapers and mirror sites often retain content after the original disappears.

Why this matters:

- Deleting is not remediation. If a file with credentials was public for six weeks, assume it was copied. Rotate the credentials; do not rely on deletion.
- Removal is a process, not a button. You can request exclusion from archives and removal from search results, but outcomes vary, and the request itself should be tracked as a ticket with an owner.
- Wayback also helps the threat-intel side. A domain that now parks a blank page may have hosted a phishing kit last month. The snapshot shows its page structure, brand targeted and form actions, which gives you indicators to hunt for.

Tools and pitfalls:

- Snapshots are partial. Missing snapshots do not prove a page never existed; archived pages may be missing scripts, images or dynamic content.
- Timestamps show when the archive captured a page, not when the content was published. Do not treat a snapshot date as the first-exposure date.
- Live links inside an archived page often point to the live internet, not to archived resources. Clicking them from a snapshot of a malicious site can still contact the malicious server. View archived malicious pages from an isolated environment.

For your research log, always save the exact archive URL, the capture time and, where policy allows, a local copy and its hash. Evidence you cannot reproduce later is weak evidence.

sections.heading: Code and Paste Search: Hunting Leaked Secrets
sections.content:
Developers publish secrets by accident constantly: an API key committed in a config file, a database password in a test script, a private key pasted into a public issue. Public code hosting search and paste sites make these discoverable by anyone, and automated bots harvest them within minutes. Defensive secret-leak hunting means finding them first.

GitHub code search supports qualifiers that scope to your organization or to strings that identify your company:

```
org:example-corp password
org:example-corp path:.env
"example-corp.com" (password OR secret OR token OR api_key)
"example-corp.com" path:**/*.yml
filename:id_rsa "example-corp"
```

The first two cover repositories your organization owns. The next three are the more important ones, because they find leaks in repositories you do not own: a contractor's project, an employee's personal repository, or a former intern's coursework containing real endpoints. Pivot terms worth searching include your internal hostnames, your email domain, your product code names and distinctive prefixes of your own key formats.

Paste sites are the other source. Pastes appear and disappear quickly, so monitoring beats one-off searching: set up alerts or a monitoring service on your domain, brand name and employee email format, and review hits daily. Search for the domain followed by terms such as password, dump, or database.

High-signal patterns include:

- Cloud provider access key IDs and secret keys, which have fixed prefixes and lengths.
- Private key headers in files with names like id_rsa or a .pem extension.
- Connection strings that include a username and password.
- Combo lists, which are credential pairs for your email domain.

Responsible handling of a found secret is the core skill, and the order matters:

- Record the location (URL, repository, commit hash, timestamp) and a minimal redacted note. Do not copy the secret into tickets or chat.
- Revoke or rotate first. The secret must be treated as compromised from the moment it was public.
- Do not test whether the credential still works against production. Checking is use, and it may be unauthorized or may trigger alarms. Ask the system owner to confirm status using their own tooling, and review their access logs for use during the exposure window.
- Remove the content, but understand that deletion does not fix anything. Git history, forks, caches and archives persist. Rewriting history is cleanup, not remediation.
- Find the root cause: why was the secret in code, and could a pre-commit scanner or push protection have stopped it?

If the secret belongs to another organization, apply the same rule as for exposed documents: do not use it, do not test it, and notify the owner or a CERT.

False positives are common. Placeholder values such as example passwords in documentation and test fixtures match the same patterns as real keys. Check entropy, format and context before escalating.

sections.heading: Building Effective Queries: Iterate, Pivot, Log
sections.content:
Good searching is iterative. Your first query is a hypothesis, the results correct it, and the second query is better. The process has a rhythm worth practicing.

**Start broad, then narrow.** Begin with site: plus a single risk term. If you get thousands of results, add exclusions (-site:www.example-corp.com, -inurl:blog) and file types. If you get zero, loosen: remove quotes, drop a filter, or test the operator on a page you know exists. A zero-result query is only informative if you have confirmed the query would have matched a known positive.

**Pivot on findings.** Every hit contains new search terms. The pivots you should reach for:

- A new subdomain found in a result becomes the next site: value.
- A document's author, creator or last-modified-by field gives employee names and username formats.
- An internal hostname or project code name found in a file becomes an exact-phrase query on code and paste sites.
- A certificate subject name found on an infrastructure engine becomes a new domain to dork.
- An IP address found anywhere becomes an org: or net: query on Shodan or Censys.

**Build a query library.** Keep reusable dorks in version control, grouped by risk family, with the date last run and the expected baseline. Rerun them on a schedule (for example monthly). The value is in diffing: a result set that did not exist last month is a new exposure, and that is far more actionable than a one-off scan.

**Keep a research log.** For every query you record:

```
Date/time (UTC) | Engine | Exact query string | Result count | Notable hits (URL) | Verdict | Follow-up
2026-11-02 09:14 | Google | site:example-corp.com intitle:"index of" | 3 | https://files.example-corp.com/backup/ | Live listing, confirmed | Ticket SEC-1042
```

The log lets another analyst reproduce your work, proves what you did and did not look at, and avoids duplicate effort. It is also your defense if a question arises later about why you accessed something.

Practical pitfalls:

- Rate limits and CAPTCHAs. If the engine throws a challenge, slow down. Do not rotate proxies to evade it; that violates terms of service and signals automation.
- Result drift. Rankings and indexes change, so screenshot or save the evidence at discovery time.
- Confirmation bias. If you only search for what you expect, you miss unexpected exposure. Vary vocabulary: not only password but also credentials, passwd, secret, token, and non-English equivalents if your organization operates in other languages.
- Scope creep. Write down your scope (domains, IP ranges, brand terms) before starting, and stop when results leave it.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Hunting Your Own Public Files and an Exposed Admin Portal
sections.content:
Scenario: you are an analyst at Example Corp (example-corp.com). A recent audit noted that marketing and engineering use many subdomains. Your manager asks for an external exposure review, with written authorization and a defined scope: example-corp.com and its subdomains. You work only with passive search.

**Step 1: map the subdomains.**

```
site:example-corp.com -site:www.example-corp.com
```

The results include files.example-corp.com, staging.example-corp.com and portal-old.example-corp.com. The last two are not in the asset inventory. Log them as unknown assets.

**Step 2: look for directory listings.**

```
site:files.example-corp.com intitle:"index of"
```

One hit: a listing at /exports/ showing several .csv files and a file named db_backup_2025.zip. You do not download anything. The listing page and its snippet are enough to establish a live, unauthenticated exposure of potentially sensitive data. You note the URL, timestamp and file names.

**Step 3: search for sensitive documents across the domain.**

```
site:example-corp.com (filetype:xlsx OR filetype:pdf) ("internal use only" OR "confidential")
```

Three results. Two are public whitepapers with a boilerplate disclaimer, which are false positives. The third is an HR salary spreadsheet on the staging host. Its snippet shows the column headers, which is enough to classify it as sensitive personal data without opening the file.

**Step 4: find login portals.**

```
site:example-corp.com (inurl:admin OR inurl:login) -site:www.example-corp.com
```

The query returns portal-old.example-corp.com/admin/ with the page title of a content management system's sign-in page. You do not attempt to log in. You pivot to the infrastructure engine:

```
hostname:portal-old.example-corp.com
```

The result shows the host presenting a product version that your vulnerability team knows is end-of-life, with a scan date nine days ago. This is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.

**Step 5: check history and code leaks.** A Wayback listing of portal-old shows it was last updated in 2023. A code search for "portal-old.example-corp.com" finds a public repository from a former contractor with a config file; you record the URL and commit hash, redact the content in your notes, and escalate it to be rotated.

**Step 6: document and remediate.**

| Finding | Severity | Remediation | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live directory listing with backup archive | High | Disable indexing, remove files, assume copied, rotate any embedded credentials | Web platform |
| Salary spreadsheet on staging | High | Take down, restrict staging behind SSO, request search removal, notify privacy team | HR systems and IT |
| Legacy admin portal, end-of-life software | High | Decommission or restrict by IP and MFA, patch if retained | Application owner |
| Contractor repository with config | Medium to High | Rotate secrets, request repo takedown, review access logs for the exposure window | Engineering and Security |
| Unknown subdomains | Medium | Add to inventory, assign owners | Asset management |

Finally, add the dorks to your query library, schedule a rerun in 30 days to confirm that the results are gone from the index, and add a control so new subdomains cannot be created without an owner and a review.

sections.heading: Legal and Ethical Boundaries, and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
Advanced search is powerful precisely because it surfaces data that owners did not mean to publish. The same skills used by a defender are used by criminals, and the only difference is intent, authorization and conduct. Anchor your practice to a few rules.

**Scope and authorization.** Searching public indexes is generally lawful in most jurisdictions, but accessing, downloading or using what you find may not be. Confirm that your organization's policy and, where relevant, your contract or program rules cover the research. For threat-intel work on malicious infrastructure, follow your team's safe handling procedure: use isolated browsers, avoid interacting with forms, and prefer archived copies.

**Other people's data.** Dorks sometimes surface exposure that belongs to a third party. The right behavior is consistent:

- Stop and do not browse further.
- Do not download, store or forward the content. Keep the minimum record of location and time.
- Report to the owner's security contact (a security.txt file at the domain, or a published disclosure policy) or to a national CERT.
- Never use credentials, tokens or personal data you find, and never test them "just to confirm".

**Data handling inside your own team.** Findings can themselves be sensitive. A research log that pastes live credentials or personal records into a shared ticket creates a second exposure. Redact and limit access.

**Technical pitfalls recap:**

- Index lag: confirm that a result is live before declaring an incident, but also confirm that a removed item is gone before closing one.
- False positives: boilerplate disclaimers, sample keys and documentation examples look like real leaks.
- False negatives: one engine, one query and one day cover little. Rotate engines and rerun on a schedule.
- Automation and rate limits: scraping breaks terms of service and can get your analysts' IP ranges blocked. Use official APIs and honor their quotas.
- Attribution errors: shared hosting, CDNs and cloud IP reuse make it easy to blame the wrong owner. Verify ownership before assigning a ticket.
- Over-trusting robots.txt and noindex: they ask crawlers not to index, they do not control access. Anything sensitive needs authentication, not obscurity.

The mindset to carry forward: search is the cheapest sensor you have. Run it routinely against your own names and domains, log what you do, verify before you escalate, fix the root cause rather than the symptom, and treat anything that was ever public as possibly copied.

quiz.question: While running a dork scoped to your company, you also run a broader query and find a live spreadsheet of another company's customer records on an open server. What is the most appropriate action?

options.label: Download the file for evidence and email it to the other company's support address
Record only the URL and timestamp, stop browsing, and report to the owner's security contact or a CERT
Open several records to confirm that the data is genuine before you write any report
Ignore it because it belongs to someone else and is outside your authorized scope

quiz.explanation: Keeping a minimal record of the location and time and then reporting through the owner's security contact or a CERT lets the owner fix the problem without you holding or spreading their data. Downloading and emailing the file creates a second copy of personal data and spreads it further. Opening records to confirm is unnecessary access to data you have no right to use. Ignoring it leaves a live exposure that you could have helped close, and responsible reporting is the accepted norm.

quiz.question: Which query best surfaces forgotten subdomains of example-corp.com that may host directory listings?

options.label: example-corp.com index of backup files with a password in the title
inurl:example-corp.com filetype:html -intitle:welcome
site:example-corp.com -site:www.example-corp.com intitle:"index of"
related:example-corp.com intext:parent directory

quiz.explanation: The site: operator limits results to the domain, the minus operator removes the main web host so that other subdomains stand out, and the quoted title phrase targets the typical heading of an automatic folder listing. The plain keyword query has no operators and is ranked by popularity. The inurl: version matches the domain text anywhere in a URL and filters on the wrong features. The related: operator no longer works as documented and does not filter by title or domain.

quiz.question: You find a live cloud access key in a former contractor's public repository that references your company. What should you do first?

options.label: Contact the owner of the account to revoke or rotate the key, treating it as already compromised
Use the key briefly against the cloud account to check that it is still valid
Ask the contractor to delete the repository and then close the ticket as resolved
Rewrite the repository history yourself and consider the exposure fully remediated

quiz.explanation: A public secret must be assumed to be copied by automated harvesters, so revoking or rotating it is the step that actually removes risk, and the system owner can then review logs for use during the exposure window. Testing the key is itself use of a credential and may be unauthorized or trigger alerts. Deleting the repository does not remove forks, caches or archives. Rewriting history is cleanup only, because copies persist and the key remains valid until rotated.

quiz.question: Your team deleted a sensitive PDF from the corporate website three weeks ago. Why can the document still be a risk?

options.label: Deleting a file from a web server always leaves a hidden copy on the server itself
The file can persist in web archives, stale search results, mirrors and downloads made while it was public
Search engines are required by law to keep every page they have ever indexed
The robots.txt file prevents any deletion from taking effect until the next crawl

quiz.explanation: Content that was public may have been captured by archive services, kept in search index entries until the next recrawl, mirrored by scrapers, or downloaded by visitors, so deletion alone does not undo the exposure. The server-side claim is incorrect, since deleting a file removes it from the server. No law obliges search engines to retain pages forever. The robots.txt file asks crawlers about what to fetch and has no power to block or delay deletion.

quiz.question: A Shodan result shows a host in your IP range with an old, vulnerable software version in its banner, last scanned nine days ago. How should you treat it?

options.label: As a confirmed exploitable vulnerability, so declare an incident straight away
As proof of nothing, because infrastructure engines are unreliable and should not be used
As a lead to verify against your inventory and scanner, since banners can be stale or spoofed
As a reason to connect to the host and test the exploit yourself to settle the question

quiz.explanation: A banner reports what the service claimed at scan time, and versions can be backported, spoofed or already fixed, so the finding needs verification through your asset inventory and authorized vulnerability scanning. Declaring an incident on an unverified banner would waste response effort. Dismissing the engine ignores a valuable source of perimeter visibility. Exploiting the host yourself goes beyond passive research and needs explicit authorization and a change process.
